info.bio: Si a cualquier escucha más o menos versado se le pide que nombre un puñado de autores que se hayan adelantado a su época con obras que escapen a toda etiqueta y que, al mismo tiempo, constituyan pruebas de fuego para lo oídos, tal lista incluiría seguramente a Captain Beefheart, Albert Ayler, Red Crayola, Ornette Coleman, The Velvet Underground y otros, dictados por el gusto personal. A esa lista debe anexarse un grupo que, por su sola intención musical, merece un capítulo aparte: The Shaggs.

scenes.name: Country-rock y roots-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En los setenta, el reajuste a los viejos valores (blues, folk, country) convierte al rock en uno de los mayores éxitos del consumismo: el Establishment ya no intenta destruirlo, lo absorbe. El country-rock de Gram Parsons es una moda enorme: Commander Cody, New Riders Of The Purple Sage, Manassas, Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Poco y los Eagles (Desperado, Hotel California); en Nashville surgen los «outlaws» (Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson). El roots-rock sigue con Hot Tuna, Little Feat y Doobie Brothers, y la nostalgia recupera el blues (Roy Buchanan, Bonnie Raitt), la armonía vocal (Manhattan Transfer, Roches, McGarrigle Sisters) y los cincuenta (American Graffiti).

podcast.title: Comparison to Nobody
podcast.body: The Christian music group "Nobody" is humorously described as "The Shags of Soul," drawing a parallel to their unique style within outsider music. "These are the Shags of Soul."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critical Acclaim and Influence
podcast.body: The Shags' album *Philosophy of the World* gained legendary status, with notable figures like Frank Zappa praising their work. In 1996, Rolling Stone magazine included the record in its lists of the 100 most influential recordings of the 20th century, one of the greatest garage rock recordings of all time, and one of the 50 most significant indie releases. "Guys like Frank Zappa started singing the praises of the shags."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cult Status and Musician Endorsements
podcast.body: Despite or because of their unconventional sound, The Shaggs are frequently name-checked by famous musicians who cite their recordings as favorite garage rock albums. They are paradoxically also described as "quite possibly the worst group to ever walk into a recording studio." "The Shags are often named checked by famous musicians, asked to name their favorite garage rock recordings of all time. They are also paradoxically quite possibly the worst group to ever walk into a recording studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Father's Managerial Vision
podcast.body: Their father, Austin Wiggins, served as their manager and producer. Despite being financially poor, he purchased instruments for his daughters and paid for their lessons. He drove them to Massachusetts to record, believing he needed to capture their sound "while they were still at their peak," despite what others might perceive as their lack of musical talent. "They were managed and produced by their father Austin Wiggins, and I'm putting air quotes around managed and produced. Despite being dirt poor, he bought his children instruments and paid for lessons. And then he drove everybody down to Massachusetts in order to get his girls on tape while they were still at their peak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kurt Cobain's High Regard
podcast.body: Despite the album's peculiar nature, Kurt Cobain notably ranked *Philosophy of the World* as number five on his personal list of the top 50 albums of all time. "Kurt Cobain ranked this album as number five on his top 50 albums of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mention in Outsider Music History
podcast.body: The Shags are listed among artists previously covered as examples of outsider music, alongside Wesley Willis, The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, and others. "On those programs, I covered Wesley Willis, the Shags, the legendary Stardust cowboy, Jandic, Captain B. Fart, Daniel Johnson, Florence Foster Jenkins, and even Charles Manson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Era Inclusion
podcast.body: The Shaggs are categorized within the original Garage Rock era, alongside The All Sisters trio. "You can put the All Sisters trio, the shags into this category."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Parental Management and Recording Drive
podcast.body: The band was managed and produced by their father, Austin Wiggins, who, despite being "dirt poor," purchased instruments and arranged lessons for his daughters. He then drove them to Massachusetts, believing them to be at their peak, to record 12 songs in less than a day. "By being dirt poor, he bought his children instruments and paid for lessons. And then he drove everyone down to Massachusetts in order to get his girls on tape while they were at their peak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneers of Accidental Lo-Fi
podcast.body: In 1969, long before lo-fi music became a deliberate genre, The Shaggs, a group of sisters from Fremont, New Hampshire, released what is considered by some to be the definitive lo-fi record of all time. "In 1969, long before people started making music that was deliberately low-fi, there was a group of sisters from Fremont, New Hampshire, who released what could be the definitive low-fi record of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Austin Wiggins Era
podcast.body: Following Austin Wiggins' death in 1975, the Wiggins daughters pursued other endeavors, as their father's constant encouragement ceased. However, their album *Philosophy of the World* subsequently achieved legendary, almost mythical status, prompting its rediscovery and critical re-evaluation. "Austin Wiggins died in 1975, and without his constant pushing, the daughters went on to other things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rapid Recording Process
podcast.body: The Shaggs recorded an entire dozen songs in less than a single day. "They recorded a dozen songs and less than a day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Worst Group in Recording Studio
podcast.body: The Shags, a trio of sisters from the Woods of New Hampshire, were frequently described as possibly the worst group to ever enter a recording studio. Despite this perception, their material is regarded as the "garageiest" within garage rock and they were name-checked by musicians as far back as the 1970s. "The shags were the three Wiggins sisters. They were managed and produced by their father Austin Wiggins, who for many accounts was just a delusional jerk."
